storyboard.claim: Charlotte passes Jack the three-column list — crucial intelligence about who stands where.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Charlotte handing a torn sheet of notebook paper (the three-column list) to Jack in a private moment.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Context established Charlotte as a covert actor; now we see the concrete act: the list.
storyboard.addedInformation: The looselafPaper icon is the book's own icon for this exact object — the literal list the narration names.

storyboard.claim: One host calls Charlotte an informant for the resistance; the other flatly rejects the label.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Charlotte standing neutral — the contested figure — while the strike callout signals the host's rejection.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the list hand-off; now the debate over what that act means begins.
storyboard.addedInformation: Strike style is correct: the narrator explicitly says 'I reject that completely' — the phrase is repudiated.

storyboard.claim: Charlotte is not a hero — she is protecting her own social status through calculated political moves.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Charlotte with a smirk: she is charming and self-serving, not innocent.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Direct counter to the 'covert hero' framing rejected in 201.
storyboard.addedInformation: Smirk signals manipulative self-interest without needing narration — the icon test passes.

storyboard.claim: Charlotte wants the internal feeling of being a good person without taking any of the external risks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Charlotte looking pleased with herself — the happy face is the internal glow she seeks, not genuine joy.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Naming the psychological mechanism behind the political behavior identified in 202.
storyboard.addedInformation: Happy face on Charlotte here is deliberate: she is self-satisfied, not kind — the muted viewer reads self-approval.

storyboard.claim: Remaining neutral in the face of organized bullying is a catastrophic failure of the moral test.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Charlotte with a blank expression — pure apathy, indifference to what is happening around her.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The verdict on the psychology named in 203.
storyboard.addedInformation: Blank = apathy/indifference (per rules); it is the correct face for someone who sees wrong and chooses nothing.

storyboard.claim: Performative pity is useless — Charlotte gives Jack the paper in secret, never in public.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Charlotte slipping the three-column paper to Jack privately, not in the open cafeteria.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets up the contrast with Summer's public action that follows in 206.
storyboard.addedInformation: The looselafPaper icon makes the secrecy concrete — a document passed in shadow rather than a public act.

storyboard.claim: Summer sits with August in public, in the light of the cafeteria — the exact opposite of Charlotte's secret act.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Summer and Auggie seated together at the cafeteria table, Summer genuinely happy.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Direct contrast to Charlotte's covert paper-passing in 205.
storyboard.addedInformation: The kitchen set maps to the cafeteria. Summer's happy expression is genuine warmth, not performative.

storyboard.claim: Charlotte stays in the shadows — doing what she is capable of, but not what is required.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Charlotte alone, blank expression, held back — the person who will not cross the threshold.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The other half of the contrast introduced in 206: Summer in the light, Charlotte in the shadow.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the 'shadows' are metaphorical; the blank face and absence from the table carry the visual meaning.

storyboard.claim: The school is being sorted in real time — Charlotte's literal three-column list is the sorting mechanism made visible.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A sorter diagram with the three columns from Charlotte's paper.
storyboard.onScreenText: The whole school sorted: Julian's side, Neutral, or Auggie's side
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The moral conclusion from the previous beat is now shown as a structural diagram.
storyboard.addedInformation: This is the one structural beat where a diagram earns its place: the book's actual three-column list maps directly to a sorter.

storyboard.claim: You are either on the side of kindness, the side of cruelty, or you are complicit through your neutrality.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Charlotte holding the list with a blank expression — the embodiment of the third column.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the three positions spelled out by the diagram in 208.
storyboard.addedInformation: Charlotte holding the list while blank-faced makes her complicity literal without the icon.

storyboard.claim: August hasn't changed — he has simply forced the entire fifth grade to reveal exactly who they are.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie standing still in the classroom — unchanged, the fixed test, while others are sorted around him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Returns the camera to Auggie after the Charlotte analysis — restates his role as the fixed moral catalyst.
storyboard.addedInformation: Auggie's neutral face is correct here: he is not acting, he simply exists and that existence sorts others.

storyboard.claim: Halloween is the one day August tries to change the rules — to manipulate the sorting mechanism through invisibility.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The mask icon: Halloween is literally about the mask Auggie wears to be unseen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pivot from the Charlotte/sorting analysis to the Halloween sequence.
storyboard.addedInformation: Mask reads as 'a false public face, pretending' — exactly what Halloween gives Auggie: one day to pretend to be unseen.

storyboard.claim: To understand Halloween you must understand August's physical reality — a life of enforced hyper-visibility.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The astronaut helmet icon: the book's own symbol for Auggie's lifelong desire for invisibility.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the Halloween deep-dive by grounding it in Auggie's body.
storyboard.addedInformation: The astronaut helmet is the book's signature object for this exact theme — no other icon captures it.

storyboard.claim: August is at the audiologist — his hearing is getting worse; he describes it as being underwater.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie sitting in a medical office (hospital set), looking sad — this IS a healthcare visit, so the medical icon reads correctly.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the abstract theme in 212 to the specific medical appointment that starts the Halloween sequence.
storyboard.addedInformation: Medical reads as healthcare/being treated — this is exactly that: an audiologist fitting.

storyboard.claim: Because August has no typical outer ears, standard hearing aids that hook over the ear cannot work for him.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie sitting in the medical office, worried — one more way his body falls outside standard solutions.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The consequence of the hearing loss established in 213.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: no icon can show 'hearing aid incompatibility'; the callout carries the information.

storyboard.claim: The doctor has to slip a massive, heavy-duty headband onto August — a highly visible alternative to normal hearing aids.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie sitting, sad, the indignity of the device visible in his face.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The solution to the problem named in 214 — and it is conspicuous, not discreet.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the rig cannot render the headband itself; the sad face and the callout carry it.

storyboard.claim: The doctor casually compares the headband to Lobot — the cyborg from The Empire Strikes Back.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie's surprised face: a doctor just compared him, offhandedly, to a sci-fi cyborg.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The doctor's careless comparison adds insult to the indignity of 215.
storyboard.addedInformation: Surprised is the right face — the comparison lands as unexpected and stinging.

storyboard.claim: August hates it — he groans, whines, crosses his arms. One more piece of constant, highly visible medical intervention.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie standing, arms crossed, angry — the body language of a child fed up with medical indignities.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: August's emotional response to the headband and the Lobot comparison from 215–216.
storyboard.addedInformation: Angry + idle with arms crossed reads as refusal and frustration — the rig can express this.

storyboard.claim: This medical reality is why the second detail is so crushing — cut to the evening of Halloween.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie in the bedroom, sad — the scene is set before we see what happened.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Scene transition from the audiologist to Halloween night — the pivot the hosts signal.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: transitional beat; the sad face and set change carry the emotional tone.

storyboard.claim: August is in bed, claiming to his mother that he is nauseous — he is hiding after what happened at school.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie lying in bed, sad; Isabel nearby, worried. The lying action with the bedroom set reads as sick in bed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: We are now inside Halloween night — Auggie is not at the door, he is in bed.
storyboard.addedInformation: lying + room set reads as ill/resting (per rules); Isabel's presence grounds the domestic scene.

storyboard.claim: The Bleeding Scream costume — the one he wore to school instead of his planned one — is crumpled on the floor.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The mask icon paired with Auggie lying in bed: the discarded Halloween mask is the image the hosts describe.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The physical evidence of what went wrong — the costume he wore, abandoned.
storyboard.addedInformation: Mask here is literal: a Halloween costume mask lying discarded — the most concrete possible reading of this icon.

storyboard.claim: Right next to the crumpled Scream mask is the Boba Fett costume Isabel spent two painstaking weeks making.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Isabel standing in the bedroom doorway, sad — the mother who made the costume that was never worn.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The second object on the floor — the intended costume versus the impulsive one.
storyboard.addedInformation: Isabel is placed first because this beat is about her sacrifice; Auggie is present in background (lying).

storyboard.claim: Daisy rests on Auggie's legs. The one day he yearns for all year — complete invisibility — was completely ruined by what he heard Jack say.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie lying in bed, sad, with the dog implied at his legs — alone with what he heard.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The emotional core of the Halloween scene: this was supposed to be his one safe day.
storyboard.addedInformation: The lying pose in the bedroom set reads as sick/resting in bed, which is exactly the scene described.

storyboard.claim: This scene raises the critical question of how August survives his reality — specifically because of what Jack said.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie alone in the bedroom, thinking — processing the betrayal he heard.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Bridges the ruined Halloween image (222) to the analytic debate about what it means (224+).
storyboard.addedInformation: Think action reads as internal processing — appropriate for a character lying awake with what he heard.

storyboard.claim: One host argues Halloween for August is actually a toxic crutch — a false escape that delays real growth.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie standing neutral — the subject of the debate the hosts are now having.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the two-host debate about the meaning of Halloween for August.
storyboard.addedInformation: Neutral face is appropriate: this beat presents the argument, not the verdict.

storyboard.claim: Halloween gives August a completely false sense of belonging — he feels like a normal kid only because he is hiding his reality.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie looking happy — but this is the illusory happiness of Halloween, not real belonging.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The mechanism behind the 'toxic crutch' label: the happiness is contingent on hiding.
storyboard.addedInformation: Happy face is intentionally ironic here — it shows the false belonging the narration names, not genuine acceptance.

storyboard.claim: As long as he relies on a mask to feel accepted, he is delaying the actual painful work of living as he truly is.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie looking worried — the painful truth underneath the Halloween happiness.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The cost of the false belonging identified in 225.
storyboard.addedInformation: Worried face signals the anxiety underneath the illusion — and that one host is pushing back hard on this argument.

storyboard.claim: The counter-argument: Halloween is the only psychological break August gets from the relentless staring of every person he passes.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie walking on the street, sad — showing the ordinary reality he lives in every day without the mask.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The rebuttal to 226 — the host defends Halloween as a necessity, not a weakness.
storyboard.addedInformation: Street set shows his daily exposed reality, making the need for the break visceral.

storyboard.claim: Imagine every single person you make eye contact with flinches or looks away or whispers — every day of your life.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie walking the street with an afraid expression — carrying the weight of relentless public reaction.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The specific daily experience that makes Halloween's break necessary.
storyboard.addedInformation: Afraid face on Auggie shows how the constant flinching from others registers on him.

storyboard.claim: Halloween is not a crutch — it is a designated mental health day. He gets to put on a mask and just breathe for a few hours.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie genuinely happy for a moment — the relief Halloween is supposed to provide.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The conclusion of the pro-Halloween argument — survival, not weakness.
storyboard.addedInformation: Happy face here is the correct emotional reading: a few hours of genuine relief.

storyboard.claim: You cannot ask a kid to be a warrior 365 days a year — he needs protection, not endless battle.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The shield icon: protection, not a weapon — what August needs and only gets one day a year.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The capstone of the defense of Halloween — you cannot expect endless fortitude from a child.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shield reads as protection — the literal thing the narration says August deserves but cannot sustain every day.

storyboard.claim: But the mask failed him — he ended up overhearing the worst betrayal of his entire life precisely because he was hiding.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie and Jack together — Auggie afraid, Jack present but unaware August is listening.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The counter-argument lands: the mask's failure is the proof the other host needs.
storyboard.addedInformation: Auggie's afraid face reads the shock and pain of the betrayal; Jack's presence is the source.

storyboard.claim: Because the world intruded on his one safe day — and the world will always intrude.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie alone on the street, sad — exposed and unprotected even on his designated safe day.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The synthesis of the mask debate: even the one safe day could not hold.
storyboard.addedInformation: Street set reinforces the public exposure that Halloween was meant to escape.

storyboard.claim: The mask allows August's face to change for one day, but ultimately proves the thesis: he cannot change his reality.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie standing on the street, sad and still — unchanged, unchangeable.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The thesis statement that Halloween's failure proves: the change must happen in others.
storyboard.addedInformation: This is the pivot point of the entire analysis — the mask debate resolves into the book's central claim.

callout.text: AROUND HIM WHEN JACK DIDNT KNOW

storyboard.claim: When Jack didn't know August was listening, Jack's true heart was revealed — the hiding enabled August to see who Jack really was.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Jack talking with a smirk, unaware Auggie is present — his unguarded self exposed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The second function of the mask: it let August see the sorting mechanism operating in secret.
storyboard.addedInformation: Smirk on Jack shows sinister charm — the face of someone saying something he would not say to Auggie's face.

storyboard.claim: The mask didn't protect August — it let him see the sorting mechanism operating in secret. That is heavy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie alone, thinking — absorbing the weight of what the mask accidentally revealed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The analytical reframe of the betrayal: not just hurt but revelation.
storyboard.addedInformation: Think action reads as internal processing — the weight of insight, not just pain.

storyboard.claim: The fixed fact of his face is inescapable — which leads to the climax where the sorting mechanism finally solidifies.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie standing still, neutral — the unchanging constant at the center of the story.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closing the Halloween chapter; pivoting toward the nature retreat climax.
storyboard.addedInformation: Neutral face is deliberate: the fixed fact is not emotional, it simply IS.

storyboard.claim: The nature retreat is the moment the entire group identity coalesces — the moral crucible of the book.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie and Jack in the forest — the setting for the climax introduced here.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the final act sequence after the Halloween analysis.
storyboard.addedInformation: Forest set establishes the dark, unfamiliar territory the narration calls 'dark alien territory' in the next beat.

storyboard.claim: Picture the outdoor movie night in the woods — it's dark, alien territory for Auggie.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie in the forest at night, worried — the darkness amplifies his usual exposure.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets the mood of the nature retreat introduced in 237.
storyboard.addedInformation: Worried face in the forest set reads as unease, isolation — the right tone before the confrontation.

storyboard.claim: August and Jack leave the main group for the bathroom and run into a group of older seventh graders from another school — led by Eddie.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Auggie and Jack walking through the forest, Auggie afraid — moving toward an unseen threat.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The inciting moment of the climax — the two boys separated from safety.
storyboard.addedInformation: Afraid face on Auggie anticipates the confrontation; the walk action shows them moving into it.
